title: AI in Legal Research: The Battle Over Copyright and Innovation — full episode transcript
pub: AI and the Future of Law / 2030 Vision, American Arbitration Association
author: Jen Leonard · Bridget McCormack

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source confirms that AI can replace substantive junior-associate research and synthesis, but it does not adopt the cluster’s concern that this will undermine expertise reproduction or call for reconstructed apprenticeship. Instead, it redirects attention toward redefining lawyers’ value around judgment, strategy and broader service provision, while expressing reduced concern about legal education.

Its contribution is predictive and demonstration-based, however, and does not establish the leadership, incentive, data or workflow conditions needed to realise that redesign.

st.t: AI copyright: Product purpose reshapes market harm
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s case-specific framing: it explains ROSS’s defeat through the product’s shared legal-research purpose, direct competition with Westlaw, and asserted training-data licensing market, while cautioning that the district court ruling does not determine frontier-model cases.
qs: They were taking Westlaw headnotes and using them to train an AI model (not a generative AI model, which we'll get into in a minute) to produce a product they would sell to the exact same market Westlaw serves (lawyers and judges).
But it's a district court case; it has no precedential value outside the District of Delaware.

st.t: Court AI: Existing failures set the comparison
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s access-oriented case for AI by predicting that AI-assisted legal research can expand service delivery, while distinguishing capability demonstrations from real-world deployment. Its support is indirect and prospective: it focuses on lawyers’ work rather than court systems and provides no measured evidence of improved justice outcomes.

kp.k: Free ChatGPT impressed construction dispute specialists in informal comparison
kp.d: McCormack reports a conference exercise using a mock construction dispute originally prepared for law school. Participants and free ChatGPT answered the same eight questions; she recalls agreement with senior experts on six out of eight, with participants divided on the other two. This is an anecdotal demonstration, without a participant count or formal validation, rather than evidence establishing reliable autonomous adjudication. She says the exercise increased previously inexperienced lawyers' openness to AI.
qs: I think their data showed it agreed with these senior experts in the field on six out of eight of the specific questions they asked it to decide.
And on the other two, the questions were really nuanced and the group was divided.

But I think I was wrong, because by doing it in the free model and showing just how good it was, this entire room of senior lawyers—many of whom hadn't really been using it regularly yet—were pretty moved by the fact that just the free version could do such a good job.

kp.k: Uneven adoption includes potentially unauthorized workplace AI use
kp.d: Leonard describes a widening experiential gap between habitual AI users and professionals who barely use it. She recalls an unspecified cross-industry employee survey published the preceding week as finding approximately 30% actively using AI professionally, and reports legal-industry conversations about undisclosed organizational use. Her survey recollection supplies neither sample size nor methodology.
qs: There was a study out last week: a new survey of employees across different industries found that I think 30% of people are actively using AI at work now for professional purposes.
Whether they're allowed to or not.
But I will say I am hearing more conversations in our industry about "secret cyborgs" as a major problem in organizations—people finding out that others are using tech for all sorts of things.

kp.k: AI competition increasingly involves legal strategy and dispute-resolution pitches
kp.d: McCormack reports an unsolicited $97.4 billion Musk-led offer rejected by OpenAI's board and attributes to commentators the interpretation that it could complicate OpenAI's nonprofit-to-for-profit conversion. She also endorses that strategic interpretation. Separately, she reports Grok 3's marketing claim to resolve disputes quickly and cheaply, explicitly saying she has not used the model; this is a reported vendor proposition, not demonstrated legal performance.
qs: Some commentators viewed Musk's unsolicited bid as an attempt to complicate that.
It is also the case that Musk has sued OpenAI to stop it from converting to a for-profit business.
I haven't used it myself, but by all accounts it's pretty sophisticated.
One of Grok 3's pitches is that it can revolutionize law and justice. It says, send your disputes to Grok 3 and we can resolve them quickly, efficiently, and inexpensively.

kp.k: ROSS ruling links training infringement to direct market competition
kp.d: Leonard describes Judge Bibas's summary judgment ruling for Thomson Reuters in litigation filed in 2020, emphasizing rejection of ROSS's fair-use defense. In her account, factor one favored Thomson Reuters because headnotes trained a commercial, non-transformative legal-research competitor; factor four weighed against fair use through effects on both legal research and emerging AI-training-data licensing markets. This is the hosts' account of the opinion, not an independent doctrinal analysis.
qs: He found that ROSS's use was commercial (trying to sell a product to lawyers for legal research) and, importantly, non-transformative.
The product ROSS was developing was intended as an actual replacement and competitor to Westlaw.
But he also noted that there's a new emerging market for licensing data for AI training.

kp.k: Public law differs from publishers' protected editorial additions
kp.d: McCormack distinguishes noncopyrightable judicial opinions from Westlaw's added headnotes; Leonard identifies the numerical taxonomy linking legal materials as the creative element. They frame this distinction as central both to the ROSS dispute and to whether alternative legal-research systems could be built from underlying public legal materials.
qs: You can't copyright the law itself; Westlaw can't just say, "We grabbed it, so we own it now."
But as all of us know who went to law school and practiced law, the headnotes are what Westlaw has added to the law—that is the protected product.
And the creative element is the numerical taxonomy that you referenced—the system lawyers use to develop connections across case law and treatises.

kp.k: Hosts caution against generalizing ROSS to generative AI
kp.d: Leonard emphasizes the trial-level ruling's limited reach and says appellate decisions and possible Supreme Court review would be more consequential nationally. Both hosts stress that ROSS involved pre-generative AI and direct competition. McCormack speculates that general-purpose model developers could distinguish their purposes and processes, while expressly disclaiming knowledge of whether they trained on Westlaw or Lexis materials.
qs: I think outside of legal circles, there's been a tendency to overstate the importance of this case in the broader tech landscape and its precedential value.
Judge Bibas was careful to note that this was a pre–generative AI case.
The frontier models—I have no idea if they trained on Lexis or Westlaw products (let me be very clear: no idea what they trained on at all; I don't think anybody knows right now).

I could imagine them saying, "We weren't doing that to build a competitor for Lexis or Westlaw. We're just trying to train a general-purpose technology, right? We're building the printing press, the steam engine."

kp.k: Copyright litigation may constrain startups without securing incumbents
kp.d: The hosts attribute ROSS's closure to the litigation, initially with McCormack qualifying that attribution as something she read. Leonard argues that the ruling could offer large technology companies a route to suppress innovation if other judges accept its reasoning. Conversely, she analogizes slow legal responses to Napster-era music disruption and predicts that access to public-domain law could make the incumbent publishers' victory temporary.
qs: ROSS is, by the way, out of business—went out of business because of this litigation, I think (at least that's what I read).
It creates a roadmap, I think, for Big Tech if they find sympathetic judges who agree with Judge Bibas's reasoning here, to stifle innovation.
That, to me, is the inherent tension between protecting original works and promoting innovation.
So to me, if I were an executive at Thomson Reuters or one of these large companies that is an incumbent, I don't take that much solace in this ruling.

kp.k: Public legal data could support new research architectures
kp.d: McCormack proposes that well-resourced frontier-model companies could collect judicial opinions directly and organize doctrine differently from Westlaw and Lexis. She identifies fragmented state and trial-court systems as a collection obstacle, not proof that comprehensive ingestion has occurred. Both hosts predict weakening paywall-based protection, but McCormack repeatedly characterizes existing comprehensive ingestion as unknown.
qs: State court can be tricky in a non-unified court system; you might literally have to go district by district to get every trial court opinion.
Assuming they can ingest all of the law without the wrappers that Thomson Reuters and Lexis have put on them, they could organize it in a brand new way.
My guess is these frontier model companies could probably produce some new ways to organize doctrine.
So paywalls, I think, will not serve as moats for long—in our industry or any other.

kp.k: Research summaries need not imply access to underlying sources
kp.d: Leonard contrasts Deep Research retrieving a public District of Delaware opinion with a report summarizing 20 Inside Higher Ed articles. When challenged about the latter's paywall, the model said it relied on public commentary beyond five free articles. This reported interaction qualifies the hosts' broader paywall discussion: output about a source does not necessarily demonstrate direct access to its contents.
qs: And it immediately produced the link to the District of Delaware's website, where I could just click on a PDF, which I then uploaded to Google’s NotebookLM and turned into a podcast to listen to.
I ran a DeepResearch report on what Inside Higher Ed wrote last year about generative AI in higher education, and it produced a summary of 20 different articles.
And it said, basically, "I cannot access the underlying information beyond the five free articles that you get. So I'm basing the summaries on other public commentary about the underlying articles."

kp.k: Deep Research performs associate-like scoping, synthesis and interpretation
kp.d: Leonard describes the $200-a-month OpenAI subscription they purchased as eliciting clarifying questions, researching for several minutes and producing reports addressing implications and nuanced perspectives. McCormack identifies cross-source connections and synthesis of legal conflicts as work traditionally assigned to associates. These are favorable firsthand impressions, not measured assessments of accuracy or completeness.
qs: I don't regret it for a minute, even though it's $200 a month, which seems like a wild amount to pay.
It will then respond to you with a series of questions—the kind you'd get from a very smart junior associate, I imagine.
You give it the answers, and then it goes off for a few minutes and does deep research and presents you with a report.

the things that it does, like you said, are so similar to what you might ask an associate to do: researching and making connections across different sources of law and synthesizing places where there's conflict or not.

kp.k: Rapid research production challenges junior work and billing economics
kp.d: McCormack recounts an unnamed law-firm partner describing an AI-produced brief as A-minus level, contrasting minutes of production with an associate's week or two. Leonard says a report on the Bibas opinion surpassed what she could have produced as a junior, or would have required weeks of billable time. They infer pressure to reconsider legal work's value and business models, without supplying audited time savings, independent quality evaluation or a specific replacement pricing model.
qs: who used it and produced what he said was an A-minus level brief.
So if you can produce A-minus-level work in minutes rather than what might take an associate a week or two...
This produced a result that I could never have produced as a junior associate.
And even if I could, it would have taken me weeks of billable time to come up with something like this.

kp.k: AI-visible thought leadership may influence law-firm client acquisition
kp.d: Leonard observes that her research report repeatedly cited Davis Wright Tremaine and Skadden. She recommends publishing more public thought leadership so research systems surface firms to prospective clients, invoking Ethan Mollick's shift from search-engine optimization to AI optimization. The client-acquisition consequence is her hypothesis based on one reported experience, not demonstrated conversion evidence.
qs: in the generated research report I got, it continually referenced public-facing thought leadership from Davis Wright Tremaine and Skadden.
And I think for law firms, this is the direction they need to be heading from a marketing and business development standpoint.
And Ethan Mollick talks about this—moving from this SEO world to an AI optimization world.

kp.k: Human value shifts toward judgment, strategy and client choices
kp.d: Leonard argues AI differs from moving books online or handwritten memos to email because it performs work that currently constitutes lawyers' value. McCormack anticipates delegating research and organization while retaining human strategic, creative and problem-solving contributions. Her optimism includes providing more legal services to more people, but the episode offers no measured access-to-justice outcome.
qs: because it's not just digitizing or automating things we used to do in an analog world. It is actually doing the things that we currently bring value to.
so we can exercise the judgment and help people solve problems in ways I still think humans can do better than technology.

But I love the idea of having a super-available, never tired, never hungry partner to do that part and then being able to think strategically and creatively with a client about the choices the client could make.
We can get more legal services to more people, which again is a huge upside.

kp.k: Medical diagnostic research supplies an analogy for professional disruption
kp.d: McCormack recalls a previously discussed JAMA study as finding frontier models better at diagnosis than doctors alone or doctors using generative models, attributing the latter result to doctors overriding model suggestions. She uses this as an analogy for lawyers reconsidering their comparative strengths. No study title, sample, effect size or methodology is supplied, and she does not present it as direct evidence about legal performance.
qs: They do a study and show that the frontier models can do better diagnostic work than human doctors—and in fact can do better diagnostic work than human doctors using the generative models.
(Because the human doctors always override the generative model's suggestions.)
It feels like that kind of moment for lawyers.

kp.k: AI-assisted education still benefits from reading primary legal materials
kp.d: Leonard says her experience reduced, without eliminating, concerns about legal education. She anticipates opportunities to help students learn through opinions using AI, while emphasizing that reading the actual judgment remained distinct and important compared with reading the generated report. This is a pedagogical possibility grounded in personal experience rather than evaluated learning outcomes.
qs: I've been really, really troubled about what this means for learning, but I think there are some really interesting ways we'll be able to use these tools and have students learn through the opinions.
Reading the actual opinion was still very different and important compared to just reading the DeepResearch report.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The speakers claim AI already performs substantial legal analysis and research, and predict changes to lawyers’ work, legal-information markets, firm marketing and legal education.
pts.d: Bridget McCormack reports that free ChatGPT substantially agreed with senior construction-law specialists in a mock dispute exercise. Jen Leonard suggests advanced reasoning models could perform still better in real deployment. Both describe OpenAI Deep Research as undertaking associate-like research, synthesis and analysis in minutes. Leonard says its report exceeded what she could have produced as a junior associate, even with weeks of billable time; McCormack argues this forces legal businesses to reconsider where human work adds value. These are task-performance and business-model claims, not quantified predictions of lawyer job losses. McCormack predicts frontier-model companies could collect public-domain law and organize doctrine differently, weakening incumbent research providers’ paywall advantages; Leonard similarly predicts a new era of engagement with legal information once those materials are gathered. Leonard also argues that the ROSS litigation could provide incumbents with a conditional roadmap for impeding competitors, while offering only temporary protection against technological change. Leonard predicts that publishing thought leadership discoverable by AI research tools will help law firms attract clients. McCormack anticipates lawyers shifting toward strategic, creative client work and delivering more legal services to more people. Leonard sees potential for AI-supported legal education while retaining direct reading of opinions. Separately, McCormack reports xAI’s claim that Grok 3 could resolve disputes quickly and inexpensively; this is an attributed product pitch, not her own demonstrated performance finding.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is primarily personal use, an informal mock-dispute comparison, a secondhand practitioner assessment and discussion of litigation—not systematic measurement of legal-market effects.
pts.d: McCormack describes a conference exercise using a mock construction dispute prepared for law-school teaching: participants and free ChatGPT answered eight questions, with reported agreement on six and divided expert views on the other two. This measures agreement in a particular exercise rather than validated adjudicative accuracy across real disputes. Leonard’s productivity comparison is retrospective personal judgment based on preparing the podcast with Deep Research, not a timed associate-versus-AI study. McCormack recounts an unnamed large-firm partner’s own assessment of an AI-produced brief as A-minus; that quality rating belongs to the partner. Leonard’s marketing inference comes from repeated citations to Davis Wright Tremaine and Skadden in her generated report, not observed client conversions. Their competition analysis draws on Leonard’s reading of Thomson Reuters v. ROSS, the speakers’ account of ROSS closing, and an analogy with music-industry disruption. McCormack initially qualifies the claim that litigation caused ROSS’s closure as something she read. Their forecasts about comprehensive legal-data ingestion are explicitly speculative: McCormack says she does not know what frontier models trained on. Leonard’s example of Deep Research locating the opinion on the court website demonstrates retrieval of one public source, not comprehensive coverage of law. Her Inside Higher Ed example also records the tool saying it relied on public commentary rather than unrestricted access to paywalled articles. Leonard cites an unidentified recent cross-industry survey estimating 30% workplace AI use; it is not a legal-sector adoption estimate. The expanded-service and educational benefits are prospective judgments rather than measured outcomes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Current-use claims refer to the 2025 episode; broader market disruption is presented as near-term but without a firm date, and depends on data availability, resources and legal developments.
pts.d: The mock-dispute exercise and the speakers’ Deep Research experiences are recent observations at the time of the episode. Their Deep Research experience uses OpenAI’s $200-per-month Pro subscription; the construction exercise uses free ChatGPT. Leonard’s suggestion that reasoning models would improve dispute analysis is expressly probabilistic. The speakers anticipate relatively rapid business-model and research-market change once public-domain legal material is collected, while acknowledging uncertainty about whether comprehensive ingestion has already occurred. McCormack notes that collecting state-court materials may require court-by-court work and assumes frontier companies have sufficient resources. Her prediction that paywalls will cease protecting incumbents is not evidence that proprietary editorial content is already freely accessible. Leonard’s litigation-based innovation concern depends on other judges accepting similar reasoning. Both distinguish ROSS’s traditional, non-generative AI and direct competition with Westlaw from general-purpose generative models, and they do not claim the decision settles pending frontier-model copyright litigation. Leonard emphasizes the five-year interval between filing and the discussed ruling as a contrast with technological speed. Her educational optimism remains qualified by the importance of reading the original opinion.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Affected groups include associates, senior practitioners, law-firm leaders and marketers, legal-research incumbents and startups, clients, the public, and law students.
pts.d: Associates face AI performance of research, synthesis and drafting tasks traditionally central to their work, with implications for billable time and firms’ accounts of professional value. The speakers do not specify headcount reductions, staffing shapes or a replacement pricing model. Senior construction lawyers and arbitrators are described as becoming more receptive after seeing a free-model demonstration. Law-firm leaders face pressure to rethink work and business models; marketers may gain visibility through thought leadership cited by AI tools, illustrated by Skadden and Davis Wright Tremaine. Thomson Reuters/Westlaw and Lexis face prospective competition from new ways of collecting and organizing public law, while legal-research startups may face litigation barriers. Clients could receive more strategic and creative human attention as AI handles source-intensive tasks. McCormack anticipates broader public availability of legal services, without identifying underserved groups or quantifying a reduction in unmet legal need. Law students and educators may gain new methods for studying opinions, while direct engagement with primary sources remains important. Leonard also identifies organizational concerns around undisclosed employee AI use, without establishing how prevalent it is in law firms.
